sentences.context: 01 — Hook
sentences.summary: det_07: Naming convention: the asterisk means staff-named. Source: TidyTuesday data dictionary (https://github.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/tree/main/data/2025/2025-03-04) Facts: animal_name with leading asterisk indicates a name assigned by shelter staff; Blank animal_name means the name was not known

raw_evidence.label: Naming convention: the asterisk means staff-named
raw_evidence.content: Per the data dictionary, an animal_name beginning with '*' was assigned by shelter staff because the animal arrived without a known name (a stray, a wildlife pickup, an owner surrender who was not named in the paperwork). Blank animal_name fields mean the name was unknown and not assigned. This is more than a footnote: in 29,787 records, 9,965 names start with '*' and 12,162 are blank, leaving only ~7,660 animals (26%) who entered the shelter with a name their human had given them. The asterisk column is a quiet measure of attachment-at-intake, and a strong correlate of intake_type (owner-surrender vs stray vs wildlife).

raw_evidence.label: Three-quarters arrive without an owner-given name
raw_evidence.content: Of 29,787 records, only 7,660 (25.7%) arrive with a name typed in by an owner. 9,965 (33.5%) start with an asterisk — given by shelter staff because the animal had no known name — and 12,162 (40.8%) are blank, meaning the animal was never given a name in the system at all. The asterisk and the blank are both consequences of the shelter taking in strays and wildlife rather than just owner surrenders.

raw_evidence.label: Owner-named cats and dogs are 41% more likely to go home
raw_evidence.content: Owner-named cats and dogs return to their owner 41.3% of the time. Staff-named ones return to owner 0.8% of the time, and blank-named ones 0.8%. Conversely, staff-named animals are adopted out at 43.1% — much higher than the 24.7% rate for owner-named (who often go home instead of being adopted). The headline live-release rate is identical at 93.2% for both owner-named and staff-named, but blank-named animals drop to 61.7% — these are dominated by wildlife, where 'live release' simply isn't the right framing. The asterisk in the data dictionary turns out to be a clean proxy for 'arrived with a human attachment' that downstream behaviour confirms.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_13 ===")
dc = df[df['animal_type'].isin(['cat', 'dog'])].copy()
def is_live(o):
    if pd.isna(o): return None
    return o not in ('euthanasia', 'died', 'disposal', 'missing')
dc['is_live'] = dc['outcome_type'].apply(is_live)

# Rate of return-to-owner by name status
dc['rto'] = (dc['outcome_type'] == 'return to owner')
dc['ado'] = (dc['outcome_type'] == 'adoption')
ag = dc.groupby('name_status').agg(
    n=('is_live', 'count'),
    rto_pct=('rto', lambda x: round(x.mean()*100, 1)),
    ado_pct=('ado', lambda x: round(x.mean()*100, 1)),
    save_pct=('is_live', lambda x: round(x.mean()*100, 1))
)
print(ag.to_string())

raw_evidence.label: Annual intake — pandemic V-curve
raw_evidence.content: Annual shelter intakes cratered during the pandemic. Long Beach took in 4,826 animals in 2017 and 4,429 in 2018. Intakes then drifted down through 2019 (4,176) before collapsing to 2,421 in 2020 and a record-low 1,842 in 2021 — only 38% of the 2017 baseline. Intakes then climbed back: 3,673 in 2022, 4,009 in 2023, and 4,411 in 2024, essentially restoring the pre-pandemic level. The two-year intake trough (2020-2021) is consistent with the national pattern documented by Shelter Animals Count, which attributes the drop primarily to fewer strays being found during stay-at-home orders rather than to fewer animals in distress.

sentences.context: 04 — Seasonality
sentences.summary: det_09: Intake conditions encode triage, not just health. Source: Long Beach Animal Care Services (https://www.longbeach.gov/acs/) Facts: LBACS uses standardised triage categories at intake

raw_evidence.label: Intake conditions encode triage, not just health
raw_evidence.content: The intake_condition factor — 'normal', 'under age/weight', 'ill mild/moderate/severe', 'injured mild/moderate/severe', 'fractious', 'feral', 'aged', 'behavior moderate/severe', 'welfare seizures', 'i/i report' — is the shelter's triage code at the door. 'Under age/weight' (6,590 rows) overwhelmingly means neonatal kittens too young to survive without a nursing queen; nationally these animals are the single largest euthanasia category at open-admission shelters and the population that bottle-feeding foster networks were built to save. 'Fractious' usually means a cat too unsocialised to be handled (a candidate for TNR rather than adoption). Triage status at intake is a stronger predictor of outcome than species or age alone.

raw_evidence.label: Kitten season — May/June peak
raw_evidence.content: Animal intake at LBACS shows a strong seasonal peak in late spring. Total monthly intakes peak at 3,297 in June and 3,235 in May, with a December low of 1,633. The seasonality is almost entirely driven by 'kitten season': underage cats (intake_condition='under age/weight', animal_type='cat') jump from 40 in January to 901 in May — a 22.5x swing — and exceed 500/month from April through October. June alone brings in 666 underage kittens, more than the entire November-February stretch combined. Kitten season is the operational reason shelters lean so heavily on foster networks and bottle-feeding programs from April to October.

month_intake = df.groupby('intake_month').size()
month_kitten = df[(df['animal_type'] == 'cat') & (df['intake_condition'] == 'under age/weight')].groupby('intake_month').size()
print('All intakes by month:')
print(month_intake.to_string())
print('Underage kittens by month:')
print(month_kitten.to_string())

raw_evidence.label: The Compassion Saves pivot (May 2019)
raw_evidence.content: On 8 May 2019 the Long Beach City Council voted 8-0 to formally adopt the 'Compassion Saves' service model, replacing the older 'no-kill' framing with a philosophy that emphasises community outreach, supportive services, foster networks, and education over a single euthanasia threshold. The pivot followed years of advocacy and at least one task force after activist accusations that the shelter was killing treatable animals — including, as task force member Anna Wong told the Long Beach Post, kittens with as little as 3-5 percent body mange. By the end of 2019 LBACS reported a 33% drop in euthanasia versus 2018 and an 88% combined dog-cat save rate. This date is a structural break in the dataset: 2017 and most of 2018 reflect the pre-Compassion shelter; 2019 onward reflects the new model.

raw_evidence.label: The 90% save-rate benchmark
raw_evidence.content: U.S. shelters share a common quantitative yardstick: a 90% live-release / save rate over a rolling twelve-month period is the threshold Best Friends Animal Society and most policy groups use to certify a shelter as 'no-kill'. The reasoning is empirical, not ideological — Best Friends estimates that no more than ~10% of incoming cats and dogs have irreparable medical or behavioural conditions that prevent rehoming, so a well-run shelter should be able to save the rest. Live-release rate definitions vary slightly by jurisdiction (some include or exclude wildlife, owner-requested euthanasia, or animals dead-on-arrival), which is why interpretation matters when comparing LBACS to other systems. As of early 2025, more than two-thirds of U.S. shelters meet the 90% benchmark.

raw_evidence.label: 2024: highest adoption rate ever
raw_evidence.content: On 9 January 2025 the City of Long Beach announced LBACS had hit its 'highest adoption rate ever' in 2024 and surpassed the 1,500-pet placement target set by the 2024 strategic plan by approximately 500 animals. The figure cited in the press release for 2022 — 1,968 placements — already represented a 194% rise from 687 placements in 2018. The 2022 toolkit included a 'Compassion Saves' framework, a fleet 'Adoption Waggin' that ran 40+ offsite events, a Foster Coordinator role placing ~500 animals in homes, themed events ('Howl-O-Ween', 'Happy Howlidays'), and donation partnerships with Bixby Animal Clinic, Paw Shoppe Pet Center, Pet Supplies Plus, Zoom Room, and Pizzamania. Mayor Rex Richardson framed the gain as the payoff of community engagement and offsite events. The dataset's last row is 31 December 2024, so it covers the entire victory lap.

raw_evidence.label: The 90% save-rate benchmark
raw_evidence.content: U.S. shelters share a common quantitative yardstick: a 90% live-release / save rate over a rolling twelve-month period is the threshold Best Friends Animal Society and most policy groups use to certify a shelter as 'no-kill'. Live-release rate definitions vary slightly by jurisdiction (some include or exclude wildlife, owner-requested euthanasia, or animals dead-on-arrival), which is why interpretation matters when comparing LBACS to other systems. As of early 2025, more than two-thirds of U.S. shelters meet the 90% benchmark.

raw_evidence.label: Trap-Neuter-Return is a population intervention, not a rescue
raw_evidence.content: Roughly one in twenty rows in this dataset has the outcome 'shelter, neuter, return' or 'trap, neuter, release' — both are TNR programs in which a community cat is sterilised, vaccinated, ear-tipped, and returned to the location it came from rather than placed for adoption. Peer-reviewed work from the University of Florida and others shows targeted TNR can drop shelter cat intake by ~66% and cat euthanasia by 83-91% over multi-year horizons, because preventing kittens never born is far more efficient than processing them once they arrive. In the LBACS data, TNR outcomes look like 'releases' but are best read as a cat-population strategy: an animal exits the shelter alive, the colony shrinks over time, future intake falls. Reading those rows as 'lost' or 'released to the wild' would mislead the reader.

raw_evidence.label: Live-release rate by species — dogs over the line, cats just under
raw_evidence.content: Live-release rate by species (live = anything other than euthanasia / died / disposal / missing): dogs 92.5%, cats 77.7%, birds 68.9%, 'wild' 32.4%, 'other' 44.4%, rabbits 81.1%, reptiles 92.2%, guinea pigs 96.5%. Dogs comfortably clear the 90% no-kill bar; cats fall ~12 points short, dragged down primarily by neonates that arrive too young to survive without a queen and by feral adults that go through the TNR pathway rather than adoption. The wild-animal save rate of 32.4% should not be read alongside cat/dog rates — these animals usually arrive injured beyond rehabilitation and the alternative isn't adoption.
raw_evidence.code:
return o not in ('euthanasia', 'died', 'disposal', 'missing')
df['is_live'] = df['outcome_type'].apply(is_live)
df_known = df.dropna(subset=['is_live']).copy()
df_known['is_live'] = df_known['is_live'].astype(int)
sp_save = df_known.groupby('animal_type').agg(total=('is_live', 'count'), live=('is_live', 'sum'))
sp_save['save_pct'] = (sp_save['live'].astype(float) / sp_save['total'].astype(float) * 100).round(1)
sp_save = sp_save.sort_values('total', ascending=False)
print(sp_save.to_string())
print()

# --- ana_10: outcome by intake_condition (cats+dogs) ---
print("=== ana_10 ===")
dc = df_known[df_known['animal_type'].isin(['cat', 'dog'])].copy()

raw_evidence.label: The 90% save-rate benchmark
raw_evidence.content: U.S. shelters share a common quantitative yardstick: a 90% live-release / save rate over a rolling twelve-month period is the threshold Best Friends Animal Society and most policy groups use to certify a shelter as 'no-kill'. The reasoning is empirical, not ideological — Best Friends estimates that no more than ~10% of incoming cats and dogs have irreparable medical or behavioural conditions that prevent rehoming, so a well-run shelter should be able to save the rest. Live-release rate definitions vary slightly by jurisdiction (some include or exclude wildlife, owner-requested euthanasia, or animals dead-on-arrival), which is why interpretation matters when comparing LBACS to other systems. As of early 2025, more than two-thirds of U.S. shelters meet the 90% benchmark.

raw_evidence.label: The 90% save-rate benchmark
raw_evidence.content: U.S. shelters share a common quantitative yardstick: a 90% live-release / save rate over a rolling twelve-month period is the threshold Best Friends Animal Society and most policy groups use to certify a shelter as 'no-kill'. raw_evidence.content: Where you go after the shelter depends heavily on what species you are. Dogs predominantly go home: 29.7% return to owner, 26.6% are adopted, 19.5% transfer to a partner organisation, only 6.7% are euthanised. Cats, in contrast, rarely go back to an owner (2.2%): 27.7% are pulled by rescues, 24.4% adopted, 18.8% euthanised, 11.9% transferred, with 9.2% leaving via TNR ('shelter, neuter, return' + 'community cat' + 'trap, neuter, release'). Birds are most often transferred to a partner (34.7%) or rescue (25.2%), with euthanasia at 24.8% reflecting non-survivable injuries. 'Wild' animals are euthanised 62.2% of the time — the closest thing the dataset has to a tragic outcome, but these are typically already badly injured when picked up. Guinea pigs (33.7% adopted, 32.0% rescued, 27.9% transferred, 2.9% euthanised) and reptiles (61.6% rescued) have notably benign outcome distributions.
raw_evidence.code:
# --- ana_08: outcome by species (pct within species) ---
print("=== ana_08 ===")
for sp in ['cat', 'dog', 'bird', 'wild', 'other', 'rabbit', 'reptile', 'guinea pig']:
    sub = df[df['animal_type'] == sp]
    if len(sub) == 0:
        continue
    print(f"--- {sp} (n={len(sub)}) ---")
    pct = (sub['outcome_type'].value_counts(normalize=True) * 100).round(1)
    print(pct.head(10).to_string())
    print()

# --- ana_09: live-release rate by species ---

raw_evidence.label: Intake condition is the strongest single predictor of outcome
raw_evidence.content: Triage status at intake separates outcomes more cleanly than species or year does. Cats and dogs entering as 'normal' have a 95.3% live-release rate. 'Under age/weight' (mostly neonates) drops to 78.5%. 'Injured severe' falls to 30.7% and 'ill severe' to just 24.9%. 'Fractious' (often unsocialised cats) is 89.9% live-release because most go through TNR. 'Welfare seizures' (animals removed from cruelty cases) hit 100% live-release on n=65 — small sample but consistent with deliberate placement. The takeaway: the no-kill benchmark works well as a goal but it must be read alongside what walks in the door. A shelter that takes more severely-injured animals will have a lower headline rate even when its medical work is identical to a shelter that takes only 'normal' intake.

sentences.summary: ana_18: Why people surrender pets. Data: longbeach.csv. Method: count frequency of values. Result: Total owner-surrender rows: 2615 Code: code/05_los_intake_subtypes.py:L29-36. [full data_table in raw_evidence]

raw_evidence.label: Why people surrender pets
raw_evidence.content: Of 2,615 owner-surrender records, 857 (32.8%) have no reason recorded. Among the 1,758 with a reason: 'owner prob' leads at 405 (the catch-all for owner-side issues), then 'move' (231), 'landlord' (133, i.e. landlord prohibits pets), 'cost' (127), 'no time' (115), 'no home' (110, owner became unhoused), 'bites' (73), 'too many' (66, often after unplanned litters), 'agg animal' (58), 'allergic' (56), 'owner died' (55), 'ill' (54), 'abandon' (34), 'agg people' (32), 'poor helth' (31), 'other pet' (22), 'new baby' (13). The top four reasons together — owner-prob, move, landlord, cost — are housing- and economics-driven, accounting for ~896 surrenders (~51% of those with a reason). 'New baby' is one of the smallest categories, contradicting the common worry that pets are surrendered when children arrive.

raw_evidence.label: Length of stay — adoption is the slow path
raw_evidence.content: Median length of stay for cats and dogs varies sharply by outcome. Adoptions take 27 days median, 48.5 days mean — the slowest live exit. Rescue/transfer pulls happen in 6 days median. Return-to-owner is the fastest: 1 day median, 3.9 days mean — most lost dogs are reunited within 24-48 hours. Euthanasia has a 0-day median (much of it is 'euthenasia required' day-of-intake for non-survivable wildlife or severe trauma cases). 'Foster to adopt' takes 12 days median. The 'missing' bucket has a 73.5-day median — these are animals whose paperwork drifted before resolution.

The top 5 ZIPs are 90805 (5,672 intakes — North Long Beach including Bixby Knolls borders), 90813 (3,024 — Central Long Beach / Cambodia Town), 90806 (2,583 — Wrigley / Bixby Knolls south), 90815 (2,334 — Los Altos / Stearns Park), 90703 (1,898 — Cerritos). 90805 alone accounts for 19.0% of all intake with a known ZIP. These are dense, lower-income, family neighbourhoods where stray density is empirically highest.

    m = re.search(r'\b(90\d{3})\b', str(c))
    if m: return m.group(1)
    return None
df['zip'] = df['crossing'].apply(zip_of)

raw_evidence.label: The single hottest intake block is the shelter itself
raw_evidence.content: Hex-binning intake coordinates at 0.005 degrees (~500 m) reveals a striking artefact: the single highest-density bin sits at 33.810N, -118.085W with 560 intakes — the location of the P.D. Pitchford Companion Animal Village shelter in El Dorado Park East. Many crossing addresses default to the shelter's own coordinates when a precise pickup location wasn't recorded (e.g., owner-surrender walk-ins). The next densest bins — 33.770/-118.195, 33.790/-118.190, 33.775/-118.180 — fall in central and west Long Beach, where genuine intake density is highest.

raw_evidence.label: The asterisk pattern is intake-type specific
raw_evidence.content: The naming convention precisely tracks how the animal arrived. Owner-surrender intakes are 76.8% owner-named — and 15.5% staff-named, presumably for animals whose owners surrendered them with no name on the paperwork. 'Wildlife' intakes are 97.0% blank — wildlife is rarely named at all. 'Stray' intakes are 35.3% blank, 21.8% owner-named (the 'lost pet' pattern, where the animal had a name on a tag), and 42.9% staff-named (truly anonymous strays who got 'Squiggles' from intake staff). 'Trap-neuter-return' intakes are 68.5% staff-named — the colony cat pattern. 'Adopted animal return' is 100% owner-named — the animal kept the name from its previous adoption file.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_12 ===")
ct = pd.crosstab(df['intake_type'], df['name_status'], normalize='index') * 100
print(ct.round(1).to_string())
print()

raw_evidence.label: The Compassion Saves pivot (May 2019)
raw_evidence.content: On 8 May 2019 the Long Beach City Council voted 8-0 to formally adopt the 'Compassion Saves' service model, replacing the older 'no-kill' framing with a philosophy that emphasises community outreach, supportive services, foster networks, and education over a single euthanasia threshold. The pivot followed years of advocacy and at least one task force after activist accusations that the shelter was killing treatable animals — including, as task force member Anna Wong told the Long Beach Post, kittens with as little as 3-5 percent body mange. By the end of 2019 LBACS reported a 33% drop in euthanasia versus 2018 and an 88% combined dog-cat save rate. This date is a structural break in the dataset: 2017 and most of 2018 reflect the pre-Compassion shelter; 2019 onward reflects the new model.

raw_evidence.label: The 90% save-rate benchmark
raw_evidence.content: U.S. shelters share a common quantitative yardstick: a 90% live-release / save rate over a rolling twelve-month period is the threshold Best Friends Animal Society and most policy groups use to certify a shelter as 'no-kill'. The reasoning is empirical, not ideological — Best Friends estimates that no more than ~10% of incoming cats and dogs have irreparable medical or behavioural conditions that prevent rehoming, so a well-run shelter should be able to save the rest. Live-release rate definitions vary slightly by jurisdiction (some include or exclude wildlife, owner-requested euthanasia, or animals dead-on-arrival), which is why interpretation matters when comparing LBACS to other systems. As of early 2025, more than two-thirds of U.S. shelters meet the 90% benchmark.

raw_evidence.label: Owner-named cats and dogs are 41% more likely to go home
raw_evidence.content: Owner-named cats and dogs return to their owner 41.3% of the time. Staff-named ones return to owner 0.8% of the time, and blank-named ones 0.8%. Conversely, staff-named animals are adopted out at 43.1% — much higher than the 24.7% rate for owner-named (who often go home instead of being adopted). The headline live-release rate is identical at 93.2% for both owner-named and staff-named, but blank-named animals drop to 61.7% — these are dominated by wildlife, where 'live release' simply isn't the right framing. The asterisk in the data dictionary turns out to be a clean proxy for 'arrived with a human attachment' that downstream behaviour confirms.
raw_evidence.code:
print("=== ana_13 ===")
dc = df[df['animal_type'].isin(['cat', 'dog'])].copy()
def is_live(o):
    if pd.isna(o): return None
    return o not in ('euthanasia', 'died', 'disposal', 'missing')
dc['is_live'] = dc['outcome_type'].apply(is_live)

# Rate of return-to-owner by name status
dc['rto'] = (dc['outcome_type'] == 'return to owner')
dc['ado'] = (dc['outcome_type'] == 'adoption')
ag = dc.groupby('name_status').agg(
    n=('is_live', 'count'),
    rto_pct=('rto', lambda x: round(x.mean()*100, 1)),
    ado_pct=('ado', lambda x: round(x.mean()*100, 1)),
    save_pct=('is_live', lambda x: round(x.mean()*100, 1))
)
print(ag.to_string())

raw_evidence.label: Owner-named cats and dogs are 41% more likely to go home
raw_evidence.content: Owner-named cats and dogs return to their owner 41.3% of the time. Staff-named ones return to owner 0.8% of the time, and blank-named ones 0.8%. Conversely, staff-named animals are adopted out at 43.1% — much higher than the 24.7% rate for owner-named (who often go home instead of being adopted). The headline live-release rate is identical at 93.2% for both owner-named and staff-named, but blank-named animals drop to 61.7% — these are dominated by wildlife, where 'live release' simply isn't the right framing. The asterisk in the data dictionary turns out to be a clean proxy for 'arrived with a human attachment' that downstream behaviour confirms.

dc = df[df['animal_type'].isin(['cat', 'dog'])].copy()
def is_live(o):
    if pd.isna(o): return None
    return o not in ('euthanasia', 'died', 'disposal', 'missing')
dc['is_live'] = dc['outcome_type'].apply(is_live)

# Rate of return-to-owner by name status
dc['rto'] = (dc['outcome_type'] == 'return to owner')
dc['ado'] = (dc['outcome_type'] == 'adoption')
ag = dc.groupby('name_status').agg(
    n=('is_live', 'count'),
    rto_pct=('rto', lambda x: round(x.mean()*100, 1)),
    ado_pct=('ado', lambda x: round(x.mean()*100, 1)),
    save_pct=('is_live', lambda x: round(x.mean()*100, 1))
)
print(ag.to_string())

raw_evidence.label: Cat+dog live-release rate by year
raw_evidence.content: Restricting to cats and dogs (the population the 90% no-kill benchmark is defined for), the live-release rate at LBACS rose from 81.3% in 2017 and 78.3% in 2018 — both below the 90% benchmark — to 86.9% in 2019 (the Compassion Saves year) and a peak of 92.2% in 2020, the only year in the dataset that crosses the no-kill threshold. The rate then settled at 84.7% (2021), 83.5% (2022), 82.8% (2023), and 84.6% (2024). Even with record adoptions in 2024, the live-release rate has not returned to its 2020 pandemic-quiet peak; the absolute number of saves grew while the percentage moved sideways, because intake volume also grew.
raw_evidence.code:
dc = df[df['animal_type'].isin(['cat', 'dog'])].copy()
def _live(o):
    if pd.isna(o): return None
    return o not in ('euthanasia', 'died', 'disposal', 'missing')
dc['is_live'] = dc['outcome_type'].apply(_live)
dc_known = dc.dropna(subset=['is_live']).copy()
dc_known['is_live'] = dc_known['is_live'].astype(int)
agg = dc_known.groupby('outcome_year').agg(
    total=('is_live', 'count'),
    live=('is_live', 'sum')
).dropna()
agg['save_rate_pct'] = (agg['live'].astype(float) / agg['total'].astype(float) * 100).round(1)
print(agg.to_string())
print()

raw_evidence.label: The Compassion Saves pivot (May 2019)
raw_evidence.content: On 8 May 2019 the Long Beach City Council voted 8-0 to formally adopt the 'Compassion Saves' service model, replacing the older 'no-kill' framing with a philosophy that emphasises community outreach, supportive services, foster networks, and education over a single euthanasia threshold. The pivot followed years of advocacy and at least one task force after activist accusations that the shelter was killing treatable animals — including, as task force member Anna Wong told the Long Beach Post, kittens with as little as 3-5 percent body mange. By the end of 2019 LBACS reported a 33% drop in euthanasia versus 2018 and an 88% combined dog-cat save rate. This date is a structural break in the dataset: 2017 and most of 2018 reflect the pre-Compassion shelter; 2019 onward reflects the new model.

raw_evidence.label: The 90% save-rate benchmark
raw_evidence.content: U.S. shelters share a common quantitative yardstick: a 90% live-release / save rate over a rolling twelve-month period is the threshold Best Friends Animal Society and most policy groups use to certify a shelter as 'no-kill'. The reasoning is empirical, not ideological — Best Friends estimates that no more than ~10% of incoming cats and dogs have irreparable medical or behavioural conditions that prevent rehoming, so a well-run shelter should be able to save the rest. Live-release rate definitions vary slightly by jurisdiction (some include or exclude wildlife, owner-requested euthanasia, or animals dead-on-arrival), which is why interpretation matters when comparing LBACS to other systems. As of early 2025, more than two-thirds of U.S. shelters meet the 90% benchmark.

sources.title: What Is No-Kill? — The 90% Save Rate Benchmark — Best Friends
facts: A 90% save rate over 12 months is the benchmark for no-kill status
No more than ~10% of incoming dogs and cats are estimated to have irreparable medical/behavioural issues
More than 2 of 3 U.S. shelters reached no-kill in 2025

raw_evidence.label: Cat+dog live-release rate by year
raw_evidence.content: Restricting to cats and dogs (the population the 90% no-kill benchmark is defined for), the live-release rate at LBACS rose from 81.3% in 2017 and 78.3% in 2018 — both below the 90% benchmark — to 86.9% in 2019 (the Compassion Saves year) and a peak of 92.2% in 2020, the only year in the dataset that crosses the no-kill threshold. The rate then settled at 84.7% (2021), 83.5% (2022), 82.8% (2023), and 84.6% (2024). Even with record adoptions in 2024, the live-release rate has not returned to its 2020 pandemic-quiet peak; the absolute number of saves grew while the percentage moved sideways, because intake volume also grew.
raw_evidence.code:
dc = df[df['animal_type'].isin(['cat', 'dog'])].copy()
def _live(o):
    if pd.isna(o): return None
    return o not in ('euthanasia', 'died', 'disposal', 'missing')
dc['is_live'] = dc['outcome_type'].apply(_live)
dc_known = dc.dropna(subset=['is_live']).copy()
dc_known['is_live'] = dc_known['is_live'].astype(int)
agg = dc_known.groupby('outcome_year').agg(
    total=('is_live', 'count'),
    live=('is_live', 'sum')
).dropna()
agg['save_rate_pct'] = (agg['live'].astype(float) / agg['total'].astype(float) * 100).round(1)
print(agg.to_string())
print()
